# Channovāda Sutta (MN 144 (PTS MN iii 263))

**ID:** MN 144 (PTS MN iii 263)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Channovāda Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** Advice to Channa
**PTS:** MN iii 263
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn144

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Channovāda Sutta* (MN 144; PTS MN iii 263) recounts the final illness and death of the venerable Channa [SuttaCentral; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Set while the Buddha resides at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove and the elders Sāriputta, Mahā Cunda, and Channa are staying on Vulture Peak, the discourse opens with Channa suffering from an excruciating, terminal disease and declaring his intention to take his own life by "using the knife" [SuttaCentral; Masefield 1994; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Sāriputta and Mahā Cunda visit Channa and attempt to dissuade him from self-destruction, offering practical support and questioning him on doctrine [Harvey 2000; von Hinüber 1996; Wayman 1997]. In a non-competitive exchange between members of the Saṅgha, Sāriputta examines Channa on the eighteen *dhātu*s (the internal and external sense spheres and their corresponding consciousnesses), confirming that Channa contemplates their impermanence, sees their cessation, and does not view them as self [Kuznetsova et al. 2012; Masefield 1994]. Mahā Cunda supplements this with an exhortation on mental stability and non-attachment [Masefield 1994; Rogell 2003].

Despite the efforts of the two senior monks, Channa carries out his suicide [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Rogell 2003]. When Sāriputta consults the Buddha about Channa's destiny, the Buddha pronounces him blameless (*anupavajja*); he explains that fault lies in discarding one physical body while taking up another through craving and attachment, whereas Channa laid down his body without grasping a new birth, having attained arahantship [Harvey 2000; Masefield 1994; Rogell 2003; Wayman 1997]. Modern scholars have frequently examined this text in analyses of early Buddhist ethics surrounding illness and suicide [Harvey 2000; Wayman 1997], as well as in historical-critical discussions regarding archaic doctrinal strata, noting its specific conceptions of consciousness and its catechistic structure [Kingsbury 2002; Radich 2007].

Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral include a canonical counterpart in the *Saḷāyatana Saṁyutta* (SN 35.87) and a Chinese parallel in the *Saṁyuktāgama* (SĀ 1266) [SuttaCentral]. Automated text-reuse data from DharmaNexus confirms this close correspondence, demonstrating extensive alignment between MN 144 (§§1.2–10.7) and SN 35.87 (§§87.0.3–87.9.3), as well as significant cross-language alignment with fascicle 47 of the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99) [DharmaNexus]. In addition, DharmaNexus records substantial Pali-internal reuse of conversational formulas on grave illness and non-clinging with the *Anāthapiṇḍikovāda Sutta* (MN 143), the *Dhanañjāni Sutta* (MN 97), and the *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22) [DharmaNexus].
